headline: Neap tides settle the Eastern Sound bite as New London holds in the high 60s
subhead: Sea bass and porgies are paying the bills at Black Point while the striper bite waits on the tide clock at Twotree Channel and Hole-in-the-Wall.
body_markdown:
We're still riding the tail of that full moon push from the 10th, and it did what big July moons do to this end of the Sound — it stacked the tides high on the flood and drained them hard on the ebb, and for a few days there the current at Twotree Island Channel was ripping so much that the drift boats out of Niantic were burning through bucktails just trying to hold bottom. New London's reading around 67.8 degrees right now, which tells you this side of the Sound is still running a good four to five degrees cooler than the water piling up off Kings Point and the western end. That gradient matters — it's why our fluke bite has been more stop-and-go than the reports you're hearing out of the Norwalk and Huntington side, and it's why the sea bass and porgies, which like it a touch cooler and don't mind structure over speed, have been the more reliable meal ticket this week.

Now we're sliding into the last quarter moon, which lands mid-week, and that means neap tides settling in behind it — smaller swings, slower current, less water moving through the rips at Hole-in-the-Wall and Black Point. That's a real shift in how you need to fish these spots. On the big spring tides last week, the bass and blues were holding tight to the current lanes, using the push to ambush bait. With the current backing off, I'd expect those fish to spread out and start working the eddies and current seams instead of sitting in the main flow — which means shorter, more precise drifts and more patience at the turn of the tide rather than working the peak of the ebb or flood.

Fluke has been the mixed bag of the week. Guys drifting Niantic Bay in 18 to 25 feet on the last of the incoming have been picking at keepers, mostly 17 to 19 inches, with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the sandy stretches off the mouth of the Niantic River. But it's been more sorting through shorts than filling coolers — the cooler water has them a little sluggish, and the better drifts have come on days when the sun's had a few hours to warm the flats before the tide starts moving. If you're going, I'd target that midday window on the incoming rather than first light right now.

Black Point has been the more consistent producer, and it's all been about the rock piles and the reef structure just off the point in 25 to 35 feet. Sea bass have been thick there, and the party boats running out of Waterford have been putting anglers on limits of fish in the 14 to 17-inch range on squid strips and Gulp crab tipped jigs, fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide when the current isn't blowing the bait off the structure. Porgies have been riding shotgun on the same drops — small hooks, sandworms or clam, and you'll fill a bucket without much drama. That bite's been steady enough that it's carrying the boats through the slower stretches on stripers and fluke.

Striped bass have been the tide-dependent story of the week. Twotree Island Channel has given up some solid fish — mid-20s to low 30s inches, with a few bigger ones mixed in — but only in tight windows around the last two hours of the outgoing, when bait gets pulled through the channel and the bass stack up on the drop-off. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig have out-produced everything else there, though a few guys working live eels along the edges at dusk have connected too. Hole-in-the-Wall has been similar — good push of bluefish mixed in with the bass on the outgoing, blitzing on peanut bunker some evenings, quiet as a church the rest of the time. It's classic ambush-point fishing: show up on the wrong tide and you'll wonder what all the talk was about, show up on the right one and it can go off fast for twenty or thirty minutes.

With neap tides settling in this week, I'm not expecting the kind of ripping current that turns Hole-in-the-Wall into a feeding frenzy — but slower water isn't necessarily bad news. It should let those bass and blues sit in the eddies longer instead of blowing through on the tide, which can actually make for a longer, more workable window if you're willing to fish it slow and let the current seams do the work instead of covering water fast. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at Twotree Channel with bunker chunks, and I'd have a Plan B lined up at Black Point for sea bass and porgies if the tide stage doesn't cooperate. McCook Point is worth a look too on the smaller tides — the current there has been gentle enough lately for porgy fishing off the beach without a boat.

Bottom line for the week: sea bass and porgies are the sure thing, fluke is a grind that rewards patience over the warmer midday tide, and stripers and blues are all about hitting Twotree and Hole-in-the-Wall on the right stage of a shrinking tide. The water's cool enough and clean enough that something's biting every day out there — you just have to be standing in the right spot when the tide says go.
